# Overview

Factor scores from categorical items can have different precision across
participants. The original 2S-PA framework accounts for this
observation-specific measurement error using definition variables
(Lai & Hsiao, 2022).

This simulation compares 2S-PA with joint categorical SEM in a two-factor
latent regression. For a worked IRT analysis, see
[2S-PA with OpenMx and IRT](tspa-vignette-mx.html).

The structural model has two correlated unit-variance factors with a single path,
`F2 ~ F1`. The stage-1 items are either **binary** (2PL) or **polytomous** (graded
response, 4 categories), and the item thresholds are either **balanced** (spread
across the latent range) or **skewed** (shifted so most responses fall in the lowest
category). The table labels identify each combination of stage-1 scoring and
stage-2 correction:

- **`tspa`** / **`tspa_mx`** — *joint* stage 1, with the pooled `tspa()` or observation-specific
  `tspa_mx_model()` stage 2, respectively;
- **`tspa_local`** / **`tspa_mx_local`** — the same two stage-2 routes, but with a *local*
  stage 1 that scores each factor from its own items separately;
- **WLSMV** — joint SEM fitted to the categorical indicators using `lavaan::sem()`.

The population standardized path is known, so we report bias and the
proportion of 95% confidence intervals containing that value (coverage).
Here, "observation-specific" means that the measurement quantities are
not pooled; the EAP score measurement model remains an approximation.

The generation script is `data-raw/sim_categorical_irt.R` (kept out of the build); it
writes the fixture read here (`vignettes/sim_categorical_irt.RDS`).

# Data-generating model

The latent model is, on the unit-factor-variance scale,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{F1} & \sim N(0, 1), \\
\texttt{F2} & = 0.6 \, \texttt{F1} + \zeta, \qquad \zeta \sim N(0, 0.64),
\end{aligned}
$$

so `Var(F1) = Var(F2) = 1`, the factor correlation is $0.6$, and the true
**standardized** `F2 ~ F1` path is $\gamma^* = 0.6$. Each factor is measured by
`5` items with discrimination $a = 1.5$.

- **Binary** items follow the 2PL, $P(Y = 1 \mid \theta) = 1 / (1 + e^{-(a\theta - b)})$.
- **Polytomous** items follow the graded-response model with `4` categories and
  thresholds $d_1 < d_2 < d_3$, where $P(Y \ge k \mid \theta) = 1 / (1 + e^{-(a\theta - d_k)})$.

The two threshold conditions shift the marginal item response:

```{r dgp, message = FALSE}
x <- readRDS("sim_categorical_irt.RDS")
meta <- x$meta
cat("gamma* (true std path) =", meta$gamma_star,
    "  n =", paste(meta$n, collapse = ", "),
    "  B =", meta$B, "\n")
cat("mean marginal item response by condition:\n")
print(round(meta$marginal, 3))
```

`balanced` is centered (binary marginal ~0.5; graded ~1.4 of 0--3) while `skewed`
concentrates responses in the low end (binary ~0.2; graded ~0.7). Skewed thresholds
provide less measurement information for many participants. This can produce
larger and more heterogeneous score uncertainty, making the treatment of
observation-specific measurement error especially relevant.

# Estimators compared

All five estimate the **standardized** `F2 ~ F1` path (the correlation between the
factors), the scale-free quantity comparable across them. They differ along two
dimensions — the **stage-1 scoring** (joint vs. local) and the **stage-2 correction**
(pooled vs. observation-specific):

- **Stage 1 — joint.** Fit the two-factor item-response model (`mirt`, `COV = F1*F2`) and
  score it with `get_fs()`. Each factor's EAP score conditions on *all* items, so the two
  factors borrow information from one another through their correlation.
- **Stage 1 — local.** Score each factor from its *own* five items with two separate
  single-factor `mirt` fits, then combine the two single-factor results into a
  block-diagonal two-factor result with `combine_fs()` (zero cross-block `fsL`/`fsT`).
  Each score then conditions only on its own items.
- **Stage 2 — pooled** (labels `tspa`, `tspa_local`): `tspa("F2 ~ F1", scores)`, which
  *pools* the per-observation quantities to a representative value before correcting the
  regression.
- **Stage 2 — observation-specific** (labels `tspa_mx`, `tspa_mx_local`): `tspa_mx_model("F2 ~ F1",
  scores)`, which uses the per-observation quantities as definition variables — the
  non-pooled correction.
- **WLSMV:** the fully joint `lavaan::sem()` of the measurement model and the path, fit
  with `estimator = "WLSMV"` on the ordered items. It depends only on the raw items, so
  it is the same reference regardless of stage-1 scoring.

The standardized path is read from each fitted model as
$\hat\gamma \, \text{SD}(F1) / \text{SD}(F2)$, with the standard error from a
first-order (delta-method) linearization in the structural path and the two factor
variances. This puts the lavaan and OpenMx results on the same SD scale.
The reported SEs do not include the additional `corrected_se = TRUE`
adjustment for uncertainty in the stage-1 measurement quantities.

# Results

`B = `r meta$B` replications at each of the `r length(meta$n)` sample sizes
(`n = `r paste(meta$n, collapse = ", ")`)). A finite point estimate was obtained in at
least `92%` of replications in every condition, and in at least `99%` at `n = 200` and
`500`. A few `n = 50` fits returned no usable standard error; those reps are excluded
from the SE and coverage statistics only (their point estimates still count toward bias).

```{r summ, message = FALSE}
res <- x$res
g <- meta$gamma_star
summ <- function(d) {
  de <- d[!is.na(d$est_std), ]
  ds <- d[!is.na(d$se_std), ]
  lo <- ds$est_std - 1.96 * ds$se_std; hi <- ds$est_std + 1.96 * ds$se_std
  c(bias = mean(de$est_std) - g, mc_sd = sd(de$est_std),
    rmse = sqrt(mean((de$est_std - g)^2)),
    mean_se = mean(ds$se_std), calib = mean(ds$se_std) / sd(de$est_std),
    coverage = mean(lo <= g & g <= hi), n_se = nrow(ds))
}
methods <- c("tspa", "tspa_mx", "WLSMV", "tspa_local", "tspa_mx_local")
```

## Point estimates

Per condition and method, bias (mean estimate minus `0.6`), the Monte Carlo standard
deviation (MC SD), and RMSE (`sqrt(bias^2 + MC SD^2)`) of the standardized path, with the
binary and polytomous items in separate columns:

```{r point-est}
pt_ns <- expand.grid(n = meta$n, skew = c("balanced", "skewed"),
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pt_ns)), function(i) {
  o <- pt_ns[i, ]
  mm <- function(it, m) {
    d <- res[res$n == o$n & res$itemtype == it & res$skew == o$skew & res$method == m, ]
    s <- summ(d); c(s["bias"], s["mc_sd"], s["rmse"])
  }
  do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, function(m) {
    b <- mm("binary", m); gd <- mm("graded", m)
    data.frame(n = o$n, skew = o$skew, method = m,
               bias_binary = round(b[1], 3), mc_sd_binary = round(b[2], 3),
               rmse_binary = round(b[3], 3),
               bias_graded = round(gd[1], 3), mc_sd_graded = round(gd[2], 3),
               rmse_graded = round(gd[3], 3), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(pt, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Point estimates (standardized path) by item type. True value = 0.6.")
```

For joint stage-1 scoring at `n = 200` and `500`, the observed biases are
small for both 2S-PA versions and WLSMV. Retaining observation-specific
measurement quantities generally reduces the downward bias associated
with pooling in these conditions. The difference is most apparent with
skewed thresholds.

Results vary more at `n = 50`. In particular, WLSMV has an upward bias
of about 0.10 for skewed binary items in this simulation. The table should
be read alongside the usable-SE counts below, because some small-sample
fits do not yield usable standard errors.

## Standard errors

Mean reported standard error, its calibration (`mean SE` / Monte Carlo SD), and the
empirical 95% coverage, per condition and method, with the binary and polytomous items in
separate columns (`n_se` = reps with a usable SE):

```{r se-table}
se <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pt_ns)), function(i) {
  o <- pt_ns[i, ]
  mm <- function(it, m) {
    d <- res[res$n == o$n & res$itemtype == it & res$skew == o$skew & res$method == m, ]
    s <- summ(d); c(s["mean_se"], s["calib"], s["coverage"], s["n_se"])
  }
  do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, function(m) {
    b <- mm("binary", m); gd <- mm("graded", m)
    data.frame(n = o$n, skew = o$skew, method = m,
               mean_se_binary = round(b[1], 3), calib_binary = round(b[2], 3),
               coverage_binary = round(b[3], 3), n_se_binary = b[4],
               mean_se_graded = round(gd[1], 3), calib_graded = round(gd[2], 3),
               coverage_graded = round(gd[3], 3), n_se_graded = gd[4],
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(se, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Standard errors (standardized path) by item type. Nominal coverage 0.95.")
```

Calibration compares the mean reported SE with the observed sampling SD
across replications; a ratio of one indicates agreement. Coverage compares
the reported confidence intervals with their nominal 95% level. Neither
quantity is uniformly ideal across conditions.

At `n = 50`, several conditions show SEs that are too small and coverage
below 95%, particularly for WLSMV with skewed binary items. Bias, imprecise
variance estimates, and the first-order standardization approximation can
all affect coverage. This simulation does not isolate their contributions.

## Joint vs. local stage-1 scoring

Separate scoring uses only the five indicators of each construct. Joint
EAP scoring can also use information from the other construct's indicators
through the estimated factor correlation. Both approaches carry their
corresponding measurement information into stage 2.

The separately scored versions show larger observed bias at `n = 50`
in this study, especially with binary items. Differences are smaller at
`n = 200` and `500`. This pattern is consistent with a benefit from
shared measurement information in small samples, but it is specific to
the correlated-factor models studied here.

# Discussion

- **Measurement error can be handled after IRT scoring.** At the larger
  sample sizes, the 2S-PA estimates are close to the population path in
  the conditions examined.
- **Pooling is a substantive approximation.** Replacing individual
  measurement quantities with an average can change the estimates,
  particularly when score precision varies substantially across people.
- **Small-sample inference remains difficult.** Measurement-error
  correction alone does not ensure well-calibrated standard errors or
  confidence intervals.
- **The stage-1 model matters.** Joint and separate scoring use different
  measurement information and show different small-sample biases here.

The study is single-group and small-scale (`B = `r meta$B`), with one
discrimination value and four categories in the polytomous conditions.
Use it as an illustration of the scoring and measurement-error choices,
rather than as a precise prediction of performance in another application.

## Reference

Lai, M. H. C., & Hsiao, Y.-Y. (2022). Two-stage path analysis with definition
variables: An alternative framework to account for measurement error.
*Psychological Methods, 27*(4), 568–588. <https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000410>
